name: Calcite
physical: Traditionally associated with a feeling of renewed energy
Crystal healers link it to comfort for bones and joints in folklore
Often kept nearby for general vitality
summary: Calcite is a common calcium carbonate in many colours, prized in crystal work as an energy cleanser and amplifier. Learn its meaning, varieties and care.
intro: Calcite may be the most versatile mineral in the shop. It is one of the most abundant minerals in the earth's crust, building limestone, marble and cave formations, yet it appears in an astonishing range of colours and forms. Rhombohedral clear crystals, honey-yellow chunks, green cubes, orange blocks, pink masses and waxy stalactites all fall under the name. Its softness, a mere 3 on the Mohs scale, makes it easy to carve into spheres and hearts, and its soft glow looks lovely on a shelf. A fine piece feels smooth and waxy in the palm, and breaks along sharp, mirror-like cleavage planes.
history: The name comes from the Latin calx, meaning lime, which is what burnt limestone becomes. Humans have used calcite-based rocks for building, plaster and mortar since antiquity, from Egyptian alabaster to Greek and Roman marble. Optical calcite from Iceland, known as Iceland spar, played an important role in early studies of light polarisation. Viking tales have been linked to sunstones of this kind, though that remains debated. Calcite has also been found in cave art contexts as natural formations. In the crystal community it has become an everyday workhorse stone, valued for its range of colours.
meaning: In the crystal tradition, calcite is a powerful amplifier and cleanser. It is said to absorb stagnant or negative energy and transform it into clear, usable energy, which is why many place it in a room to refresh the atmosphere. Each colour carries its own meaning, but all calcites share a theme of clarity, motivation and energetic renewal. White and clear calcite are linked with calm and spiritual connection, yellow with confidence, orange with creativity, green with healing growth, blue with serenity and pink with love. Practitioners also use calcite when feeling stuck or lethargic, believing it helps start fresh momentum. It is generally considered a gentle, beginner-friendly stone.
howToUse: Place a calcite piece on your desk to keep the energy bright during study or work. Use a chunk or sphere in the corner of a room as a decorative energy refresher. Hold a piece during meditation and visualise stale energy draining away. Pair it with other stones in a grid to amplify their intention. Carry a small tumbled stone in your pocket when you need a motivational lift. Because it is soft, keep it away from jewellery wear, and choose a pendant or display rather than a ring.
care: Calcite is soft and dissolves in acids, so keep it away from water soaks, vinegar, lemon, perfume and cleaners. Wipe gently with a soft dry cloth, and if needed a barely damp one, then dry at once. Cleanse by smoke, sound, or placing it on selenite, and charge under moonlight. Avoid long exposure to strong sun, which can fade the colour. Store it separately in a soft pouch, since quartz and most other stones will scratch it. Keep dry and avoid damp rooms.
identify: Genuine calcite scratches easily with a copper coin and fizzes in dilute acid. Clear pieces show double refraction, a doubled image seen through the crystal. Many bright colours on the market, such as vivid blue and green, are dyed. Wax or glass can imitate carved pieces, and onyx marble or alabaster may be sold under the name. A hardness of 3 and rhombohedral cleavage are good clues. Natural colours tend to be soft and slightly cloudy rather than neon.

faq.a: In crystal tradition, calcite is used to cleanse and amplify energy and to support motivation and calm. Each colour has its own focus. These are metaphysical beliefs, not medical claims.
Avoid soaking calcite. It is soft and reacts to acids, so water, vinegar and cleaners can dull the surface. Wipe it with a soft cloth and cleanse with smoke, sound or selenite instead.

faq.q: How do I tell calcite from quartz?
faq.a: Calcite is much softer, so a copper coin or steel blade scratches it, and it fizzes in dilute acid. Quartz is hard and glassy and will scratch glass. Calcite also has rhombohedral cleavage and often a waxy or pearly sheen.
